analysis.one_liner: Bars colleges that take federal aid from forcing students into arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would restore students' right to sue their college, was never voted on and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The CLASS Act would have stopped colleges that participate in federal student aid from requiring students to sign away their day in court. It would make mandatory arbitration clauses unenforceable in enrollment agreements and bar schools from restricting students' right to sue, join a class action, get a jury trial, or choose the courtroom. Students would keep full access to the courts when their college wrongs them.
analysis.who_benefits: Students — including current and former students of colleges, and especially for-profit colleges, that use mandatory arbitration — would regain the right to take their school to court, sue as a group, and have a jury hear their claims. Roughly 80% of for-profit college enrollment agreements contained arbitration clauses, which typically block class actions and often require students to travel to distant venues.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students with claims against their colleges

how_it_helps.text: Makes the federal Arbitration Act inapplicable to enrollment agreements between students and institutions of higher education, so mandatory arbitration clauses would no longer be enforced [S3].

Adds a condition to colleges' participation in federal student aid: they cannot require or enforce any restriction — including on choice of law, jury trial, or venue — on a student's ability to pursue a claim in court, alone or with others [S3].
Takes effect one year after enactment, giving colleges time to change their enrollment paperwork [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges — particularly for-profit and career colleges that rely on arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court and away from class actions — would face lawsuits they currently block, including the cost of defending group claims. Some schools warn these costs get passed on through tuition.

drawbacks.text: Removing arbitration shifts disputes into the court system, which is slower and costlier for colleges; schools would likely pass some of that cost on through tuition [S3].

For an individual student with a small claim (a few hundred or thousand dollars), arbitration can be faster and cheaper than a court case, so the bill trades that option for the right to sue and join class actions [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: when a school defrauds thousands of students at once, as for-profit college scandals have shown, only a class action can hold it accountable, and arbitration clauses are built to prevent exactly that. The cost — more litigation and some tuition pressure — is genuine but modest compared with what students give up under the status quo. On balance this is a straightforward consumer-rights measure for students.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees for its entire life — referred to Education and Labor and Judiciary in November 2021, then to subcommittees in November 2022 — and never got a markup, committee vote, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Maxine Waters introduced the bill on November 18, 2021, joined by five original cosponsors: Reps. Bass, Tlaib, McCollum, Davis, and Garcia [S3].
The Speaker referred it to the Education and Labor Committee and, in addition, to the Judiciary Committee [S5].

On November 1, 2022 — nearly a year later — it was referred to the Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law Subcommittee and the Courts, Intellectual Property, and the Internet Subcommittee [S5].
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023; the bill never reached the House floor or the Senate [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges that use mandatory arbitration clauses — for-profit colleges in particular — keep the status quo: students still cannot take them to court or join class actions over enrollment disputes.

industries.note: These schools use mandatory arbitration clauses most heavily; the bill would let students sue them in court and bring class actions, ending a major shield from accountability. Schools' interest in keeping that shield runs directly against students' ability to recover.

All federal-aid colleges would lose the ability to enforce arbitration, jury-waiver, and venue restrictions in enrollment agreements. Public and nonprofit schools face less exposure but would also bear litigation costs they may pass to students.
